claims.text: Successful formation of noble metal–based high-entropy alloy nanoparticles is primarily governed by synchronization of metal-precursor reduction.
Nearly simultaneous reduction of all metal species synchronizes nanoparticle nucleation.
Synchronized nucleation produces a homogeneous, single-phase alloy.
Disparities in precursor-reduction timing facilitate phase separation or elemental segregation.
Phase separation or segregation caused by mismatched reduction timing undermines catalyst performance.
A rapid temperature jump or strong reducing agent can accelerate and synchronize reduction of all metal precursors relative to slower processing.
A synchronized initial nucleation event can kinetically lock metal atoms into a mixed, single-phase nanoparticle.
Atomic diffusion can promote phase separation in noble metal–containing quinary nanoparticles.
Concurrent nucleation minimizes compositional gradients among constituent metals.
Slower or mismatched reduction permits early-reduced species to form separate nuclei and initiate inhomogeneous growth.
The interplay between reduction kinetics and atomic diffusion determines final alloy homogeneity.
Alloy homogeneity governed by reduction kinetics and diffusion determines the availability of surface-exposed noble-metal sites important for catalysis.
Rapid reduction will yield predominantly homogeneous, single-phase nanoparticles with uniformly distributed noble-metal atoms.
Rapid reduction will yield controllable, catalytically active surface morphologies.
Slower, sequential reduction will make phase segregation, elemental clustering, or core–shell morphologies more likely.
The proposed mechanism applies when precursor reduction potentials are sufficiently similar for an external intervention to synchronize reduction.
Extremely disparate reduction kinetics or strong ligand and surfactant effects can prevent the proposed synchronization mechanism from applying.
The mechanism is restricted to nanoscale systems in which rapid nucleation can kinetically trap an alloy configuration.
Favorable processing parameters can enable complete in-situ alloy formation from mixed elemental feedstocks.
No quantitative degree of reduction-rate synchronization required for homogeneous alloy formation is specified.
